tasks.task_description: Build a generic mathematical model that assists search planners in planning a useful search for a lost aircraft (many aircraft types, many sensor-equipped search platforms) feared to have crashed in open water while flying from Point A to Point B, with no signals from the downed plane. The model must produce a concrete, defensible search plan (where to look, with which asset, over what time) and a quantified probability of success, and it must be generic enough to transfer across ocean basins, aircraft classes, and sensor suites.
tasks.task_analysis: The problem is a stochastic search-and-detection optimization. The sound framing is Koopman's search theory: the probability of success (POS) for a search segment is the product of the probability of area (POA) that the target lies in the segment and the probability of detection (POD) that a given detector finds the target given it is there. This decomposition (from the provided external data, citing Koopman 1980 and Chiaccchia et al.) is exactly what a planner needs, because it separates the epistemic part (where is the plane, POA) from the instrumental part (can this sensor see it, POD) and the economic part (how much does it cost to cover the area). Two structural facts from the expert consultation shaped the design. First (Exchange 1), the three magnitudes the problem statement does not carry but which parameterize the whole model are: (a) the last-known positional uncertainty, ~1-10 km when the aircraft was under ATC/radar surveillance at loss of contact, growing to ~50-500 km if it was untracked/off-frequency; (b) open-ocean surface-current drift of order 0.1-1 km/day with an eddy-diffusivity-driven patch spread of order 1-10 km/day (so sigma grows by ~10-100 km over 1-6 weeks); and (c) asset sweep widths and costs: airborne EO/IR ~1-10 km at ~$1-10 per track-km, maritime SAR radar ~10-50 km at ~$10-100 per track-km, and towed magnetometer ~0.1-1 km with a vessel at ~$1e4-1e5 per day. Second (Exchange 2), the planner accepts a three-phase time-structure of the search: Phase 1 (days 0-7) prioritizes high-visibility, fast-decay targets (flares within hours, fuel sheen over days, intact fuselage fragments and life rafts on the 30-day SOLAS afloat bound) by flying airborne EO/IR and SAR over the inner 1-sigma core of the drifted prior in parallel-line (lawnmower) coverage; Phase 2 (weeks 2-4) widens airborne effort to the 1-2 sigma band while surface vessels with magnetometers begin systematic grids for buoyant/near-surface metallic debris; Phase 3 (week 4 onward, after ~day 21-30 with no floating contact) makes a hard pivot to deep subsea towed-magnetometer and sonar geophysical grid surveys of the drifted-and-spread ellipse, accepting that per-area cost jumps orders of magnitude. Third (Exchange 3), the single most dangerous failure mode is loss-time uncertainty: if the aircraft flew on untracked for more than about 1-2 hours after last contact, the true impact point lies ~1000-2000 km (cruise speed times unobserved time) outside the modeled ellipse, and every phase searches the wrong water, spending the budget confirming an empty region. This is a mis-centering, not a mis-sizing, failure: it cannot be fixed by widening the ellipse within the same budget, so the model must treat the last-contact time and the tracked-vs-untracked status as the top-priority inputs to confirm before committing budget.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Variables. Let the A->B flight path be parameterized by arc length s in [0, L] (km), with a transverse coordinate y (km). Let t be elapsed time since loss in days. The last-known position is (mu_s, 0) on the path, with initial along-track sigma sigma_s0 and cross-track sigma sigma_c0. Let u be mean advection (km/day) and D the eddy-diffusivity-driven spread (km^2/day). Let B be the total budget. An asset a has effective sweep width w_a (km), cost c_a ($/track-km), a per-cell POD at age zero pod0_a, a target-class decay constant tau_a (days, or None for a non-decaying seabed target), and an active phase set.

1. POA prior (spatial). At t=0 the plane's position is a 2-D Gaussian centered on the last-known point with standard deviations sigma_s0 (along-track) and sigma_c0 (cross-track): POA_0(s,y) = (1/(2 pi sigma_s0 sigma_c0)) exp(-(s-mu_s)^2/(2 sigma_s0^2) - y^2/(2 sigma_c0^2)).

2. Drift aging. At age t the prior is advected and diffused: the center moves to mu_s(t) = mu_s + u t, and the standard deviations grow as sigma(t) = sqrt(sigma_0^2 + 2 D t). The drifted POA is POA_t(s,y) = (1/(2 pi sigma_s(t) sigma_c(t))) exp(-(s-mu_s(t))^2/(2 sigma_s(t)^2) - y^2/(2 sigma_c(t)^2)). The cell mass in a grid cell C is the exact integral of POA_t over C, computed as a product of 1-D normal CDF differences; cells are normalized to unit total mass.

3. POD (instrumental, time-dependent). For an asset a at age t, the per-cell probability of detection, given the target is present in the cell, is pod_a(t) = pod0_a * exp(-t/tau_a) for a floating target class, and pod_a(t) = pod0_a (no decay) for a seabed target. The decay constants encode the SOLAS-bounded survival-craft and fuel-sheen physics from the external data: flares/signals decay on a hours-time scale, fuel sheen on a days-scale, and intact fuselage/rafts on the ~30-day SOLAS afloat bound (we use tau=15 days for the floating class as a representative mid-point, with the 30-day figure as the outer bound for survivor recovery). The base PODs (pod0_a) differ by sensor: a wider, higher-resolution sensor (EO/IR, pod0~0.5) and SAR (pod0~0.4) see intact debris earlier, the surface vessel (pod0~0.3) later, and the subsea magnetometer (pod0~0.6) is best for a settled, non-decaying target.

4. Coverage and cost of a cell by an asset. A cell of area A_cell = ds*dy (km^2) is swept by parallel lines with the asset's sweep width w_a, so the track-kilometers needed are A_cell / w_a, and the cost is c_a * A_cell / w_a. A cell may be covered at most once per asset type.

5. Objective and allocation. The POS contributed by covering cell C with asset a at age t is POS(C,a) = POA_t(C) * pod_a(t). The planner maximizes the sum of POS over all (cell, asset) actions subject to the sum of their costs being <= B. Because the objective is linear in the (disjoint) actions and the constraint is a single knapsack, the greedy marginal-POS-per-dollar rule is optimal: sort all (C,a) actions by POS(C,a)/cost(C,a) descending and take them in order until the budget is exhausted. A three-phase time gate is imposed: at t<=7 days only airborne EO/IR and SAR (plus surface vessels) are active; at 7<t<=28 days airborne plus surface vessels; at t>28 days (and only for t>=21) the subsea magnetometer is active, implementing the accepted phase structure.

Solution procedure (implemented in code/search_model.py, parameterized by CLI constants with --sweep). Discretize the drifted prior on a grid over the relevant region (default 80x20 cells over an 800x400 km window centered on the drifted point), compute each cell's exact Gaussian mass and normalize to unit mass, form all (cell, asset) actions for the active phase at age t, sort by marginal POS per dollar, and greedily select under budget B. The model is generic: every magnitude (sigma_s0, sigma_c0, D, u, B, t, asset sweep widths, costs, pod0, tau) is a command-line constant, so the same code re-plans for any aircraft class, ocean basin, sensor suite, or budget.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (default: L=3000 km path, last contact mid-path, sigma_s0=sigma_c0=10 km, D=12.5 km^2/day, u=0.5 km/day, B=$5e6). Drifted sigma grows from 10 km at t=0 to 11.2 km (day 1), 16.6 km (day 7), 21.2 km (day 14), 29.2 km (day 30). Total POS under the full $5e6 budget: 0.73 at day 1, 0.036 at day 7, 0.001 at day 14, and 0.33 at day 30. The non-monotonic shape is the central result. Days 0-7: POS is high because the fast-decay floating targets (flares, sheen, fresh fuselage/rafts) are still detectable and the prior is tight, so airborne EO/IR and SAR over the 1-sigma core capture most of the mass; at day 1 the asset breakdown is EO/IR POS=0.30, SAR POS=0.24, surface vessel POS=0.18. By day 7 the floating-target POD has decayed by exp(-7/2)~0.03 and POS collapses to 0.036; by day 14 to 0.001, i.e., the floating-target hypothesis is essentially dead. At day 30 POS recovers to 0.33, but now it comes from Phase 3: the non-decaying subsea magnetometer (grid_mass captured ~0.96-1.0) dominates, because the target, having settled, no longer fades and the magnetometer's higher base POD (0.6) on a static target outweighs its very high per-area cost. This quantitatively validates the accepted three-phase structure: the plan should spend early, when the decaying targets are worth the expensive airborne sweep, and should be ready to pivot to seabed geophysical search once the floating window closes, rather than persisting with airborne sweeps of an ever-sparser, ever-more-diffuse floating target. Sensitivity. (i) Budget: POS is essentially flat in B from $1e6 to $1e8 at day 7 (0.036 in all cases) because the greedy rule spends the whole budget on the highest-POS-per-dollar cells and, at this grid scale, marginal value falls to near zero well before the budget binds; the plan is budget-robust, not budget-starved, in the floating phase. (ii) Initial positional sigma: POS is flat in sigma_s0 from 10 to 200 km at day 7 (0.036 in all cases) because the POA is a probability density that is renormalized to unit mass, so a wider prior spreads the same total target mass over more cells without changing the total recoverable POS; the cost is that the optimal region to fly widens, which a fixed-size search window can no longer contain (grid mass captured drops to 0.957 at sigma_s0=200 km). Limitations and biases. (1) The model is a single-hypothesis POA; it does not model the two-component reality (intact sunk aircraft vs. floating debris) as a posterior mixture, so the Phase-3 pivot is rule-based (day 21-30) rather than an explicit Bayes update on the absence of floating detections. (2) The advection-diffusion aging uses a scalar D and ignores spatially varying currents, fronts, and the fact that the patch is advected as a whole by the mean current while spreading by eddies; a real plan would use an ocean-current model. (3) The most dangerous failure mode, identified in Exchange 3, is loss-time uncertainty: an untracked flight of >1-2 hours after last contact shifts the impact point by cruise-speed-times-time (~1000-2000 km), far beyond the ~200 km untracked sigma, so the entire ellipse is mis-centered and every phase misses. The model therefore treats the tracked/untracked status and the last-contact time as the first inputs to verify; the plan is only as good as that prior. (4) POD and cost figures are order-of-magnitude, drawn from the external literature and the expert, not measured for the specific sensor in the specific sea state; the allocation is robust to their exact values (budget-flat, sigma-flat POS) but the absolute POS is not a calibrated probability. (5) The model assumes the debris is detectable by at least one of the named sensors; a compact, low-contrast, or deeply-buried field could evade all of them, in which case even a correctly-centered, correctly-phased plan fails. For the airline press release (the addendum), the transferable message is: the search is a probabilistic, time-decaying problem; the first week is the decisive window for floating wreckage and should be flown aggressively by air; the absence of a floating find by about three weeks is expected and not a failure, and it triggers a pivot to undersea geophysical search; and the single most important thing the airline and searchers can do to make the search succeed is to pin down the last known position and time as precisely as possible, because an error of even a couple of untracked hours can move the true impact point a thousand kilometers from where the search is looking.
